Pavia, 1525

24 February, in the walled Visconti hunting park north of the city. The battle on the real ground, with a source behind every mark.

Solid: the location is stated by a cited source. Dashed: a modern historian's reconstruction, cited. Dotted: placed by this page to fit the narrative; no source gives it.

    How many were there?

    Every figure below is plotted as its source gives it, not averaged. Click a mark to see the source and passage. Where sources disagree, that disagreement is the finding.

    How this map is made

    A short guide to reading the page and judging what it shows.

    What each mark means

    Every unit, line and arrow says where its position comes from. Solid: a source of the period or a cited study states the place. Dashed: a named modern historian reconstructs it. Dotted: this page placed it to tell the story, and no source gives it. Unit sizes are not to scale.

    Each statement in the phase panel carries a dot: filled for well attested, half-filled where the sources agree on the event but not on the details, dashed for a modern reconstruction, dotted for uncertain.

    Where the ground comes from

    Rivers, buildings, roads and the town are today's, from OpenStreetMap; relief from the EU-DEM elevation model. What stood in 1525 is drawn in ink; anything later is grey and can be switched off in Layers. The park wall is traced segment by segment on ditches, roads and boundaries that follow a plan of about 1530.

    How the sources are used

    Accounts written in 1525 or soon after (letters, dispatches, chronicles, memoirs) come first; modern studies are cited as such. Numbers are shown source by source and never averaged. Where sources disagree, both versions are given, and for the main fighting the map lets you switch between two reconstructions.

    Limits

    Some key works could not be read in full (Konstam 1996, Guinand 2025, Testi 2024, the first part of Prato 1894–95); claims taken from them at second hand are marked. Dates are Julian, as in the sources. Clock times are calculated here from the sun's position and the Italian way of counting hours from sunset.

    Where each piece of data comes from

    Every place, line and unit on the map, with the source of its position. Click any tag to open the source.

    Sources

    Contemporary accounts come first, then modern studies. Each note says what the source is good for and where it is biased.
